blocks.text: Paper 1 prints a cluster: plaintiff, affidavit, injunction, adjournment. Candidates who write 'medicine' because the words look difficult have walked into the favourite WAEC trap. Those four words belong to a courtroom. Register is the language of a situation, and the situation here is law.

blocks.markdown:
**Register** is the variety of language that fits a particular situation. It changes because three things change:

- **Field** — what is going on (law, medicine, a football match).
- **Tenor** — who is talking to whom (judge to counsel, doctor to patient, coach to players).
- **Mode** — speech or writing, a text message or an official report.

The same person uses different registers in one day: a student explains a diagnosis to a nurse in the sick bay, then shouts *offside* on the field, then writes *I wish to apply* to the principal.

blocks.title: Occupational register
blocks.text: An occupational or specialist register is the set of words a profession uses so that insiders can be exact. *Plaintiff* is not a stylish synonym of *person*; it is the party who brings a civil case. Using the wrong field word is not just inelegant — it is inaccurate.

blocks.title: Matching a cluster to its field
blocks.prompt: Which field do these words belong to: fallow, irrigation, seedling, livestock?

steps.text: Read each word for the activity it names, not for how 'hard' it looks.
Fallow is land left unsown. Irrigation is watering crops. A seedling is a young plant. Livestock are farm animals.
All four sit on a farm. The field is agriculture.
Reject medicine: none of these is a body, a drug or a procedure.
Reject law: there is no court, party or document. Difficult vocabulary is not a field.

blocks.answer: Agriculture — every word names a farming process, plant or animal.

blocks.markdown:
### Choosing the exact word

Sometimes the paper does not ask for the field. It asks which specialist word completes a sentence.

- In court, the party who is sued is the **defendant**, not the patient.
- A doctor writes a **prescription**, not an injunction.
- A reporter meets a **deadline**, not a fixture.
- A player is ruled **offside**, not adjourned.

If two options look possible, ask which field the rest of the sentence has already chosen, and stay inside it.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: When a cluster is listed, name the activity all the words share before you look at the options. One medical-looking word in a legal cluster is usually the distractor, not the theme. When a sentence has a blank, read the whole situation — courtroom, ward, farm, pitch, newsroom, lab — and only then pick the word.

points: Register is language fitted to field, tenor and mode.
Occupational register uses exact specialist words, not stylish synonyms.
WAEC favourites are law, medicine, agriculture, ICT, journalism and sports.
Match a cluster by the activity every word shares, not by how difficult the words look.
In a gap-fill, stay inside the field the rest of the sentence has already chosen.
